ArXiv cs.AI.title: The Cost of Saying Hello: An Empirical Study of Handshake Overhead in AI Agent Communication Protocols
ArXiv cs.AI.description:
arXiv:2610.30151v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Every interaction between AI agents begins with a handshake: the initiating agent must locate its counterpart, learn what it can do, and establish a session before the first useful message can be sent. Surveys of agent communication protocols name handshake overhead as an efficiency criterion, yet none report measurements. This paper presents the first empirical, phase-decomposed benchmark of the handshake in three major agent protocols: MCP (in both its 2025 initialize and 2026 discover eras), A2A, and ACP. ArXiv cs.AI.description:
arXiv:2610.30157v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents require interfaces to interact with external systems such as files, APIs, databases, and cloud services. Two competing paradigms have emerged: CLI (Command Line Interface), where agents execute shell commands directly, and MCP (Model Context Protocol), a structured JSON-RPC protocol providing governed, typed tool access. This paper presents a comparative analysis across 14 evaluation dimensions, supported by worked examples, security assessment against established compliance frameworks, and economic modeling. arXiv:2610.30170v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Canada's increasing wildfire activity requires frequent national hazard mapping to guide proactive mitigation, including fuel management, land-use planning, infrastructure protection, and evacuation routing. However, process-based wildfire simulation frameworks (e.g., BurnP3 and BurnP3+) rely on computationally intensive Monte Carlo simulations to model burn probability, fire intensity, and rate of spread. ArXiv cs.AI.title: When Stable and Preferred Semantics Agree: A Path-Based Approach
ArXiv cs.AI.description:
arXiv:2610.30176v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We investigate structural conditions under which preferred and stable semantics agree in abstract argumentation frameworks. Our approach is based on suitably chosen sets of paths in the attack graph and binary relations induced by them. We establish a general path-based criterion for semantic agreement and instantiate it with several classes of paths, obtaining sufficient conditions expressed in terms of well-foundedness of the corresponding relations.

ArXiv cs.AI.title: Feedback That Backfires in Games: Do LLM Players Repeat the Move They Just Watched Fail?
ArXiv cs.AI.description:
arXiv:2610.30205v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When an LLM agent's move fails, the harness writes the move and the failure message into the transcript and asks again. In tool calling, this record makes small models more likely to repeat the failed action. We test whether the same holds in games (Sokoban, Connect Four, Othello), where a move can fail by being illegal or by being legal but losing, both verified exactly. ArXiv cs.AI.description:
arXiv:2610.30277v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While artificial intelligence has made rapid progress in mathematical reasoning, many open problems depend on structure that is revealed only through large-scale computational exploration and analytical synthesis. One such example is Lehmer's problem from 1933. It asks whether the Mahler measure of an integer polynomial, which measures how far its roots stray from the unit circle, can be made arbitrarily small. ArXiv cs.AI.description:
arXiv:2610.30351v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models often apply complex reasoning indiscriminately, leading to overthinking on simple tasks and underthinking on harder ones. We present Route-and-Generate (Rouge), a hierarchical training framework that enables LLMs to adaptively decide when and how much reasoning is required for each input. ArXiv cs.AI.title: Soft Ontology Priors over Latent Concept Posteriors for Weakly Supervised Neuro-Symbolic Learning
ArXiv cs.AI.description:
arXiv:2610.30391v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neuro-symbolic (NeSy) predictors that supervise only the task label suffer from reasoning shortcuts: distinct concept mappings achieve the same maximum likelihood, leaving the recovered concepts unidentifiable and unsafe for downstream reuse. We attack this failure by injecting a soft ontology prior over the latent concepts into the training objective and compiling it together with the task constraint into a smooth, decomposable probabilistic circuit. ArXiv cs.AI.description:
arXiv:2610.30429v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their adaptability to evolving task requirements. Although recent approaches enable dynamic orchestration, trajectory-level rewards they apply assign one outcome to each decision, ofen struggling to identify the contributions of individual structural changes. ArXiv cs.AI.description:
arXiv:2610.30436v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sixth-generation (6G) communication systems are expected to support immersive, intent-driven, and latency-critical services through tight integration of multimodal intelligence, edge computing, and autonomous network control. In this setting, agentic AI systems can reason over heterogeneous inputs, use tools and network functions, coordinate across distributed entities, and adapt to dynamic environments. ArXiv cs.AI.title: SpecMAGIC: Specification-Guided Multi-Task Generalization in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
ArXiv cs.AI.description:
arXiv:2610.30443v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-task generalization is an important yet underexplored problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). Many real-world applications require multi-agent systems to generalize across complex, temporally extended tasks with diverse inter-agent coordination requirements. We introduce a specification language that combines temporal-logic task specifications with operators for expressing such requirements. We propose SpecMAGIC, a hierarchical framework that leverages the automaton structure of task specifications for subtask decomposition.

ArXiv cs.AI.description:
arXiv:2610.30445v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI agents capable of autonomous decision-making introduce significant challenges related to safety, alignment, accountability, and human oversight. Existing Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) and responsible AI approaches provide important foundations, but many remain fragmented across system design, governance, and operational deployment. This paper presents a Three-Pillar (3P) model and framework for developing safe and trustworthy AI agents through transparency, accountability, and trustworthiness. ArXiv cs.AI.description:
arXiv:2610.30450v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it with an incorrect one. Deciding when to stop is a metareasoning problem: the model must weigh what further reasoning could achieve against its cost, given what it can already answer. Direct utility training learns a stopping representation at a chosen token price; supporting new prices can require additional controller training. ArXiv cs.AI.title: Why Bother Me Again? Benchmarking Personal Agent Memory for Interaction Preferences
ArXiv cs.AI.description:
arXiv:2610.30485v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personal intelligence systems are taking on increasingly complex everyday tasks, yet repeated questions, unnecessary confirmations, and unwanted outreach can turn capable assistance into interaction burden. Reducing this burden requires agents to remember how users want to be assisted. However, existing memory benchmarks focus on factual recall and personalized answers and rarely test how agents learn and act on interaction preferences.
